meta.blurb: A secret inspector. A run-down mountain lodge. A snowstorm that closes the only road. Poppy came to judge Cedar Lodge, but four days of burnt soup, bursting pipes and Cal's smile may change what she writes.
meta.bible: Poppy Lindqvist: a secret Inspector of hotels for the Fernley Guide, about twenty-nine, honest, restless, once a restaurant cook; she has moved all her life and registers as Ms Lane. Cal Brennan: the manager, cook and handyman of Cedar Lodge, about thirty-two, warm, tired and stubborn. Rosalind Brennan: Cal's late grandmother, who ran the lodge for forty years; her rule is that nobody should spend Christmas alone. Cedar Lodge: a small timber mountain inn with a leaking roof, a sulking Boiler and a fine view of the pines. Pinecrest Mountains: the mountains. Harrow Road: the only road up to the lodge, closed by the Snow. Biscuit: Cal's old brown dog. Stanley Whitcomb and Ivy Whitcomb: an elderly couple who have come every Christmas for forty years and got engaged at the lodge forty-five years ago; Stanley cheats at games. Dana Alvarez and Ken Alvarez: parents of the eight-year-old twins Theo and Leo. Margo Adair: Poppy's editor at the Fernley Guide. Fernley Guide: the travel guidebook whose stars can make or break a hotel. Timeline: Poppy arrives a week before Christmas; the storm lasts four days; the Plough opens the road on Christmas morning. Poppy's review gives four stars. Key words: Plough, Quilt, Woodshed, Snowshoes, Inspector, Lodge, Review, Pipe, Stars, Pastry, Cellar, Blizzard, Drifts, Snowman. Voice and tone: warm, funny and cosy, a slow-burn romance with a happy ending.

B1B2: Poppy Lindqvist is a secret inspector for the Fernley Guide, which tells travellers where to stay. A week before Christmas, her editor sends her to a small mountain inn called Cedar Lodge.
The road to Cedar Lodge winds up into the Pinecrest Mountains for hours. The snow falls thicker with every mile, and Poppy grips the wheel and wishes that she had brought chains.
At dusk she finally sees a crooked wooden sign that reads Cedar Lodge, half buried in snow. A good inspector never gives her real name, so she has decided to arrive as Ms Lane.

The door is opened by a tall man with flour on his shirt and a sleepy brown dog at his heels. He says that his name is Cal Brennan, and that he is the manager, the cook and the person who fixes things.
Her room is small and cold, and cold air whistles through a gap in the window. But the patchwork quilt is thick and soft, and the view of the snowy pines is beautiful.
That evening the radio in the lounge crackles with some very bad news. The Harrow Road is closed by snow, and the storm will last four days, so nobody can leave the lodge.

There are six other guests at the lodge, and every one of them is friendly. Stanley and Ivy Whitcomb, an elderly couple, have come every Christmas for forty years, while the Alvarez family has two very noisy eight-year-old twins.
At dinner the soup tastes burnt, and Cal apologises three times before the bowls are empty. The bread, however, is warm and golden and the best Poppy has ever tasted.
At nine o'clock the power goes out, and the whole lodge falls dark. Cal lights candles and builds up the lounge fire, and the guests share stories until midnight.
Late that night Poppy finds Cal washing a mountain of dishes alone. She picks up a cloth, because she once worked in a restaurant kitchen, and they talk quietly while they work.
In the morning Cal and Poppy dig a path through deep snow to the woodshed. He laughs at her thin city boots, and she throws a handful of snow at him.

Cal tells Poppy that the lodge belonged to his grandmother Rosalind, who died last spring and left a lot of debts. A good review in the Fernley Guide would save the place, he says, and Poppy feels her stomach twist.
Before lunch the twins disappear, and the whole lodge goes out to search the grounds. Poppy and Cal find them at last inside a snow fort, cold but proud and very hungry.
After supper the guests play a noisy board game by the fire. Cal and Poppy are on the same team, and Stanley Whitcomb cheats so badly that everyone shouts.
Ivy Whitcomb has sharp eyes, and she sees how often Cal looks across the room at Poppy. She winks at Poppy over her teacup, and Poppy blushes.
On the third morning a pipe bursts in the cellar and water sprays everywhere. Cal and Poppy fix it together, soaked to the skin and laughing like children.
That afternoon Poppy watches Cal wrap Stanley's sore knee and then read a long story to the twins. He does everything quietly, as if kindness were an ordinary part of the day.
Poppy opens her notebook that night, and her list of faults is long. The list of good things is longer, and she has no idea how to put the two together.
On the fourth day the storm slowly eases, and Cal takes Poppy up a trail on snowshoes. At the top they stand together and watch the sun go down over a hundred white peaks.

Cal points to the lit windows far below and says that his grandmother Rosalind had one rule. Nobody should spend Christmas alone, she always said, and he wants the lodge to stay open for anyone who has nowhere else to go.
Poppy tells him that she has always been on the move, first as a child and now for work. She has never stayed in one place long enough to call it home.
Cal turns toward her, and for a moment they are very close. Then the twins come crashing up the trail, shouting that they have built a snowman and dressed it in Cal's best apron.
On Christmas Eve the whole lodge decorates a tall cedar branch in the lounge. Everyone makes something by hand, and the twins glue glitter onto almost everything, including the dog.
Ivy and Stanley tell the room how they became engaged at Cedar Lodge forty-five years ago, during a snowstorm just like this one. Stanley was so nervous that he dropped the ring in the soup.
Cal takes his grandmother's old recipe book from a shelf, and he and Poppy bake her famous apple pie together. Somewhere between the peeling and the rolling, a flour fight begins.
On the staircase, Poppy's phone finds a weak signal, and her editor, Margo Adair, calls at once. Margo wants the review by the end of the week, and she wants to know what the lodge is really like.
Poppy says the word inspector, and then that the heating is poor and the pipes are old. At the bottom of the stairs, Cal stops dead with a tray of mugs in his hands.
In the kitchen Cal asks her quietly whether she is the inspector from the Fernley Guide. Poppy has told so many small lies in her job, but she cannot tell this one, and she says yes.
Cal says that he thought she had been kind because she liked him, and not because she was working. He asks her to leave him alone, and his voice is very quiet.
Poppy sits alone in her cold room on Christmas Eve, feeling like the worst person in the world. After a while, old Biscuit pushes the door open and lies down on her feet.
Ivy Whitcomb knocks and brings a pot of hot tea on a tray. She tells Poppy that the truth can hurt, but a person who tells it kindly is giving a gift.
Poppy sits at the little desk by candlelight and writes all night. Her first draft is cold and correct, and she tears it into pieces because it is not the whole truth.

By dawn she has written a review that lists every fault honestly, from the cold rooms to the old pipes and the burnt soup. It also says that Cedar Lodge is the warmest place in the mountains, and it gives four stars.
On Christmas morning a big yellow plough rumbles up the Harrow Road and clears a path. The road is open at last, but not one guest asks for their bill.
Poppy packs her bag and prints the review in the lodge office. She leaves it on Cal's desk with a note that says, Please read this before I send it.
Cal finds the pages and reads them standing up in the kitchen. His hands shake a little, because it is not at all what he expected.
Ivy Whitcomb takes one look at his face and points toward the door. She tells him that if he lets that young woman drive away, he will regret it for forty years.
Poppy drives slowly to the end of the lane and stops at the gate. She looks in the mirror at the lodge, with its smoking chimney and its glowing windows, and cannot make herself go on.
Cal runs down the lane through the deep snow, still wearing his apron, and bangs on her car window. Poppy winds it down, and she is already crying.
Cal says that her review is the kindest and truest thing anyone has ever written about the lodge. He is sorry that he shut her out, he tells her, because he was frightened.
Poppy says that her name is Lindqvist and not Lane, and that none of her feelings were false. Cal laughs and kisses her in the snow beside the car.
Hand in hand, Cal and Poppy walk back up the lane toward the lodge. Every window is full of faces, and the guests cheer so loudly that Biscuit begins to bark.
Christmas dinner is served at one long table that stretches the whole length of the dining room. The turkey is golden, the soup is not burnt at all, and Rosalind's apple pie is gone in ten minutes.
After the holiday Poppy sends the review to Margo, who loves it. Margo then offers her a big promotion and a new job in a city far away.
Poppy thinks about it for one night and then calls Margo back. She says that she will write about places for the Guide from Cedar Lodge, and that she is tired of hiding who she is.
When the review appears in the Fernley Guide, bookings pour in from all over the country. By the spring the lodge is nearly full, and Cal has enough money to mend the roof.
Stanley and Ivy Whitcomb book their rooms for the next ten Christmases, just to be safe. The twins send Poppy drawings of the lodge, and Biscuit appears in every one.
In the summer Poppy takes over the bookings and the website, and she writes her articles at the front desk. She has never stayed anywhere so long, and she has never felt so much at home.
In December the first heavy snow falls on the mountains, and the Harrow Road closes again. Cal and Poppy look at each other and smile, because they have secretly been hoping for it.
On Christmas Eve, a year after she arrived, Poppy stands at the window with Cal while the snow falls. Her name is now painted on the sign by the door, and she wants to be nowhere else.
C1C2: Poppy Lindqvist spent her working life pretending to be an ordinary guest, for she was a secret inspector for the Fernley Guide, whose stars could make or break a hotel. A week before Christmas her editor, Margo Adair, gave her one last assignment, a remote and reputedly shabby mountain inn called Cedar Lodge. Poppy packed a suitcase, a notebook and her usual doubts about the whole business.

The road to Cedar Lodge twisted ever higher into the Pinecrest Mountains, and with every mile the snow came down more thickly, until the windscreen wipers could scarcely keep pace. Poppy gripped the wheel with both hands, peering through the white swirl for the faint outline of the road. She had inspected castles and palaces in her time, but never before had she felt so far from the world.

At dusk she found the lodge at last, a long timber building with snow heaped on its roof and a crooked wooden sign swinging in the wind. Warm yellow light glowed in the windows, and woodsmoke curled from the chimney into the darkening sky. A good inspector never gave her real name, so she had decided to arrive as Ms Lane, a stranger with a booking and a tired smile.

The door was opened by a tall, tousled man with flour on his shirt and an elderly brown dog leaning against his knee. He introduced himself as Cal Brennan, adding with a crooked grin that he was also the cook, the receptionist and the only person in the building who knew how to bully the boiler. The dog, whose name was Biscuit, examined Poppy's boots with great seriousness and then sneezed.

Her room was small and chilly, with a draught that whistled through a gap in the window frame and a radiator that gave off more sighing than heat. Against all this, however, stood a patchwork quilt of astonishing thickness, and a view across the snow to a black army of pines. Poppy took out her notebook and wrote the first two lines of her report, one in each column.

That evening the old radio in the lounge crackled out a warning that the Harrow Road had been closed by drifting snow. The storm, said the announcer in a voice of cheerful doom, would last at least four days, and no one in the Pinecrest Mountains should attempt to travel. Poppy looked at the window, then at Cal, and realised that she was trapped in a building she had come to judge.

Six other guests were stranded with her, and they gathered around the lounge fire as though they had known one another all their lives. Stanley and Ivy Whitcomb, a silver-haired couple in matching cardigans, had spent every Christmas at the lodge for forty years, while Dana and Ken Alvarez were trying, without much success, to manage their eight-year-old twins, Theo and Leo. Poppy shook every hand in turn, and kept her friendly smile firmly in place, as an inspector should.

At dinner the soup arrived with a distinct flavour of smoke, and Cal apologised so many times that the guests began to feel sorry for him. The bread, however, was warm and golden and astonishingly good, with a crust that crackled and a crumb as soft as a cloud. Under the tablecloth, Poppy wrote one word in her notebook, and then, after a moment's hesitation, a second.

At nine o'clock the power failed, and the whole lodge sank into a velvet darkness that smelled of woodsmoke and wet wool. Cal lit a dozen candles and built up the lounge fire until it roared, and the guests drew their chairs into a circle and traded stories well past midnight. Poppy, who had never in her life stayed up late in the company of strangers, found that she did not want to go to bed.

Late that night Poppy found Cal in the kitchen, scrubbing a mountain of pans by the light of a single lantern, and without being asked she picked up a towel. She had worked in restaurant kitchens as a student, she explained, and she had never lost the habit of rescuing anyone who looked as exhausted as he did. They talked quietly while the pans clattered and gleamed, and she forgot, for an hour, that she was supposed to be taking notes.

In the morning the snow lay waist deep around the lodge, and Cal and Poppy spent two hours shovelling a path to the woodshed. He teased her without mercy about her elegant city boots, which were by now full of snow, and she retaliated with a well-aimed snowball that burst on his shoulder. It was a long time since Poppy had laughed outdoors, and she could not remember the last time that anyone had made her do it.

Sitting on the woodpile, Cal told her that the lodge had belonged to his grandmother Rosalind, who had died the previous spring and left behind a tangle of debts and a roof that leaked in five places. A kind word in the Fernley Guide, he said, would bring enough bookings to keep the place alive, and he spoke of it with the longing of a man describing a miracle. Poppy stared down at her frozen boots, feeling like a thief, and for once in her career she said nothing at all.

Just before lunch the twins vanished, and the whole lodge, from the elderly Whitcombs to the frightened parents, spilled out into the snow to search. It was Poppy who noticed the tiny footprints leading behind the woodshed, and Cal who crawled into the half-collapsed snow fort and found two small, shivering, entirely unrepentant boys inside. He carried one on his shoulders and Poppy carried the other, and the whole party returned for hot chocolate.

After supper the lodge divided itself into teams for a ferociously competitive board game, with Cal and Poppy on the same side and the twins keeping the score. Stanley Whitcomb cheated so shamelessly, with his wife acting as his accomplice, that the room dissolved into protests and laughter every few minutes. Poppy discovered, to her considerable surprise, that she had not enjoyed an evening so much in many years.

Ivy Whitcomb had sharp blue eyes that missed nothing, and she had observed how often Cal glanced across the room at their quiet visitor, and how quickly he looked away. When Poppy caught her gaze, the old lady raised her teacup a fraction of an inch and winked. Poppy turned the colour of the fire and pretended, with great concentration, to study the game board.

On the third morning a pipe burst in the cellar, and a fountain of icy water leapt across the stone floor. Cal and Poppy wrestled with a wrench and a roll of tape, working in a wet, frantic partnership that ended only when the last drip had stopped. They stood facing each other, drenched and gasping with laughter, and neither of them seemed in any hurry to move.

That afternoon Poppy watched from the doorway as Cal wrapped Stanley's aching knee in a warm cloth and then settled by the fire to read a long adventure story to the twins, doing all the voices. He did these things quietly and without any fuss, as if kindness were simply one more chore on the list. She realised that she had never seen anyone run a hotel in quite this way.

That night Poppy opened her notebook and surveyed the damage: the draughty windows, the leaking roof, the burnt soup, the temperamental boiler, all of them real, all of them recorded in her neat hand. Yet the other column was longer, and it was filled with a different kind of fact that no star rating could capture. For the first time in her career, she did not know how to write a review.

On the fourth day the storm finally lost its strength, and Cal strapped a pair of snowshoes onto Poppy's feet and led her up a narrow trail behind the lodge. At the top of the ridge they stood side by side and watched the sun sink behind a hundred white peaks, which blushed pink, then violet, then slowly grey. Poppy, who had seen the finest views in six countries, thought this the loveliest of them all.

Cal pointed to the small golden squares of the lodge windows, far down in the blue shadow of the valley, and told her that Rosalind had kept one rule above all others. Nobody, she used to say, should be left to spend Christmas alone, and she had opened the doors to every stray traveller, widow and lost soul who happened to find the road. He wanted, more than he had ever wanted anything, to keep that same light burning through the long mountain winters.

Poppy heard herself telling him things that she had never told anyone, about a childhood spent in six towns and four schools and a succession of rented rooms. Her work, she said, had simply continued the pattern, an endless line of other people's hotels, and she had never once stayed anywhere for Christmas. Cal listened without looking at her, which somehow made it much easier for her to go on speaking.

Cal turned toward her, and the cold air between them seemed suddenly to hum, and for a long moment neither of them breathed. Then the twins came crashing up the trail, shrieking that they had built the finest snowman in the history of the mountains and had dressed it in Cal's favourite apron. Poppy burst out laughing, partly from relief and partly from disappointment, and Cal groaned.

On Christmas Eve the whole lodge gathered in the lounge to dress a great cedar branch that Cal and Ken had dragged in from the woodshed. Each guest made a decoration by hand, from paper stars and dried orange slices to a lopsided clay angel, and the twins applied glitter to everything in reach, including Biscuit. By evening the lopsided tree glittered so brightly that it almost hurt to look at it.

Ivy and Stanley told the room how they had become engaged at Cedar Lodge forty-five years earlier, during a blizzard very like this one. Stanley had been so nervous, Ivy said, that he dropped the ring into the soup and fished it out with a spoon while the whole dining room watched. The story was clearly a favourite, and they told it together, interrupting each other with great affection.

Cal took his grandmother's battered recipe book from its shelf, and together he and Poppy set about baking Rosalind's famous apple pie for Christmas dinner. Somewhere between the peeling of the apples and the rolling of the pastry, an ill-considered handful of flour was thrown, and the kitchen became a snowstorm of its own. They emerged from the battle white from head to foot, and happier than either of them had been in years.

On the landing of the staircase, the single spot where her phone could find a signal, Poppy heard her editor's brisk voice demanding the review by Friday. Margo wanted the truth, as she always did, and she wanted it in plain language with a clear number of stars at the end. Poppy, with her back to the wall, lowered her voice and tried to sound like a professional.

Poppy heard herself say that the heating was poor, that the pipes were old, and that she was, after all, an inspector with a duty to be honest. A sound like a breaking cup came from the foot of the stairs, and she turned to see Cal standing quite still with a tray of mugs in his hands. His face, which had been so open and warm only a moment earlier, had gone as blank and white as the snow.

In the kitchen, with the door closed, Cal asked her in a low and careful voice whether she was the inspector from the Fernley Guide. Poppy had told a great many small lies in the course of her work, but she found that she could not tell this one, and she answered with a single word. Yes, she said, and the silence that followed was the longest of her life.

He said that he had believed she was kind because she liked him, and not because she was making notes for a guidebook that could end his family's story. Poppy tried to explain that she had stopped taking notes days ago and that none of it had been false, but every word sounded like an excuse. Cal asked her, politely and very quietly, to leave him alone, and she did.

Poppy sat alone on the edge of her bed on Christmas Eve, shivering in the draught, and feeling like the least honest person in the whole Pinecrest Mountains. After a long while the door nudged open and Biscuit padded in, climbed with a grunt onto the bed and lay down across her feet. His warm weight did more to comfort her than any speech could have done.

A soft knock sounded, and Ivy Whitcomb came in with a tray of hot tea and a plate of shortbread. She settled herself in the only chair and announced that she had never seen two people look so wretched over such a small thing. The truth could sting, she said, but when it was told with kindness it was among the greatest gifts one person could offer another, and Poppy drank her tea and began to think clearly.

Poppy sat at the little desk with a candle at her elbow and began to write, and her first draft emerged as cold and correct as a tax return. It listed every fault of the lodge in order of severity, and mentioned nothing of the bread, the quilt, the stories or the man who kept the light burning. She read it through once, tore it carefully into small pieces and began again.

By dawn she had written the review she should have written from the start, which named every fault without mercy, from the leaking windows to the burnt soup and the boiler that sulked. It also described, in plain and careful words, a place where strangers became a family within three days, and it awarded four stars with a note that the missing one could be earned by a good plumber. She read it over, and for the first time in her career she felt proud of a page.

On Christmas morning a huge yellow plough came grinding up the Harrow Road, throwing a white wave of snow aside, and the driver blew his horn in triumph. The road was open at last, and yet not a single guest asked for their bill or even glanced toward their luggage. The Whitcombs, in fact, calmly ordered a second pot of tea and settled deeper into their armchairs.

Poppy packed her bag in five minutes, for she had never owned much, and then crept into the little office to print the review on the lodge's elderly machine. She left it on Cal's desk, squared neatly on the blotter, with a note that said only that he should read it before she sent it anywhere. Then she carried her bag out to the car in the cold, bright morning, without saying goodbye to anyone.

Cal found the pages an hour later, and read them standing at the kitchen counter with the dog leaning against his legs. His hands began to tremble somewhere in the second paragraph, for it was not at all the cold judgement he had feared, but a love letter disguised as a report. When he reached the last line, he had to put the paper down and look out of the window.

Ivy Whitcomb took one look at his face, put down her teacup with a decisive click and pointed toward the door. If he let that young woman drive away, she said, he would regret it for forty years, and she would never forgive him for letting a good Christmas go to waste. Cal did not stop to find his coat or his gloves, and he left the room at a run.

Poppy drove slowly to the end of the lane, where the lodge's crooked sign hung beside the gate, and stopped the car with the engine still running. In the mirror, the long timber building sat smoking beneath its blanket of snow, every window glowing, and she found that she could not make her foot press down. Somewhere ahead lay the road, her work and her usual life, and none of them looked like home.

Down the lane came Cal at a floundering run, still wearing his flour-covered apron, plunging through drifts that reached his knees and shouting her name to the empty mountains. He reached the car out of breath, with snow in his hair and his hands bare and red, and rapped on the window with one frozen knuckle. Poppy wound the window down with an unsteady hand, and found that she was already crying.

Cal told her, between gasps, that her review was the kindest and truest thing anyone had ever written about Cedar Lodge, and that he would repair every fault on her list before the spring. What he was truly sorry for, he said, was shutting her out, because he had been frightened of how much it mattered that she had not told him the truth. Anger, he had discovered that morning, was only fear wearing a heavier coat, and he had no further use for it.

Poppy told him that her name was Lindqvist and not Lane, that she had stopped taking notes on the second day, and that nothing she had felt at the lodge had been false. Cal laughed, a cracked and joyful sound, climbed straight over the snowbank to open her door and pulled her out into the white air. Then he kissed her, while the snow settled on their shoulders like a blessing.

Hand in hand, they walked back up the long lane toward the lodge, and every window was crowded with beaming faces, from the twins pressed flat against the glass to Ivy Whitcomb, who was dabbing her eyes with a napkin. The applause that greeted them at the door was so loud that it sent the snow sliding off the roof. Biscuit, who felt that he had been neglected in all the excitement, barked until he lost his voice completely.

Christmas dinner was served at one long table that stretched the whole length of the dining room, with candles down the middle and paper crowns on every head, including the dog's. The turkey was golden, the soup was not burnt in the slightest, and Rosalind's apple pie vanished in under ten minutes, to the loud and sincere admiration of all. Stanley rose with his glass to propose a toast to the lodge, and to the stranger who had come to inspect it.

After the holiday Poppy sent her review to Margo Adair, who read it twice and called back within the hour to say that it was the finest report she had ever received. She followed this praise with an offer, a senior position at the head office in a city on the other side of the country, with a salary that made Poppy blink. It was exactly the kind of offer that she would have accepted in a heartbeat a month earlier.

Poppy thought about the offer for a single night, walking the length of the snowy lane and back, and then telephoned Margo to say that she would not be taking it. She proposed instead to write about small inns and lodges from a desk at Cedar Lodge, openly and under her own name, since she had grown tired of pretending to be someone else. Margo, after a long pause, said that it was the most sensible idea she had heard all year.

When the review appeared in the new edition of the Fernley Guide, bookings began to pour in from every corner of the country, and the telephone that had so seldom rung now rang all day. By the spring the lodge was nearly full, the roof was mended in all five places, and the old boiler had been replaced by a gleaming new one that Cal named Rosalind. When he introduced the boiler to the guests by name, Poppy managed to keep a straight face for almost a full minute.

Stanley and Ivy Whitcomb booked their rooms for the next ten Christmases, announcing that they intended to live long enough to use every one of them. Meanwhile the Alvarez twins sent a steady stream of enormous crayon drawings, in all of which the lodge was surrounded by smiling snowmen and an unusually large dog. Poppy pinned every one of them to the wall behind the front desk, until the whole wall was a gallery.

Through the long green summer Poppy took charge of the bookings and the website, and she wrote her articles on a laptop at the front desk, between the arrival of one guest and the departure of the next. She had never stayed anywhere for so many months in her life, and she noticed with a start that she had stopped counting the days until she left. The lodge, with all its faults and draughts and cheerful chaos, had quietly become her home.

In December the first heavy snow of the year drifted down across the Pinecrest Mountains, and by evening the Harrow Road had closed once more. Cal and Poppy stood side by side at the lounge window and exchanged a look of the purest guilty satisfaction, because they had both been secretly hoping for exactly this. Nothing in the world, they agreed, could possibly be more cosy than being snowed in at Cedar Lodge.

On Christmas Eve, exactly a year after she had first stumbled through the lodge door, Poppy stood at the window with Cal's arm around her shoulders and watched the snow fall on the quiet pines. Her name was now painted on the sign beside his, beneath the words that Rosalind had always lived by, that nobody should spend Christmas alone. For the first time in her life, she did not need to go anywhere to feel that she had arrived.
